results.name: shared_divisor_rule_yes_rate
results.description: For 2+ example sets whose examples are all multiples of some m in 3..10, yes rate for non-example targets that are multiples of such a shared m; observed < null means people extend arithmetic (multiple-of-m) rules less than the model, observed > null means more.
results.code:
# name: shared_divisor_rule_yes_rate
# description: For 2+ example sets whose examples are all multiples of some m in 3..10, yes rate for non-example targets that are multiples of such a shared m; observed < null means people extend arithmetic (multiple-of-m) rules less than the model, observed > null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    hit = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
    for mm in range(3, 11):
        allm = ((ex % mm == 0) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1) & (n >= 2)
        hit = hit | (allm & (t % mm == 0))
    sel = hit & ~inset
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float)[sel].mean())

results.name: very_near_minus_moderate_near
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets 1-3 from the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 4-10 away; the model's intervals imply a monotone decline (positive value), so observed < null means people generalise relatively less to immediate neighbours than to moderately near numbers, observed > null means a steeper local gradient.
results.code:
# name: very_near_minus_moderate_near
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets 1-3 from the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 4-10 away; the model's intervals imply a monotone decline (positive value), so observed < null means people generalise relatively less to immediate neighbours than to moderately near numbers, observed > null means a steeper local gradient.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    dist = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = r[(dist >= 1) & (dist <= 3)]
    b = r[(dist >= 4) & (dist <= 10)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: recency_nearest_example
results.description: For 2+ example sets and non-example targets, yes rate when the nearest example is the last-shown one minus yes rate when the nearest is the first-shown one; the model is order-invariant, so observed < null means people generalise less around the most recent example (primacy), observed > null means a recency advantage.
results.code:
# name: recency_nearest_example
# description: For 2+ example sets and non-example targets, yes rate when the nearest example is the last-shown one minus yes rate when the nearest is the first-shown one; the model is order-invariant, so observed < null means people generalise less around the most recent example (primacy), observed > null means a recency advantage.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    last = ex.ffill(axis=1).iloc[:, -1]
    first = ex.iloc[:, 0]
    dl = (t - last).abs()
    dfst = (t - first).abs()
    base = (n >= 2) & ~inset
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = r[base & (dl < dfst)]
    b = r[base & (dfst < dl)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: mixed_parity_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets after 3+ example sets containing both odd and even numbers (no parity rule fits); observed > null means people generalise more broadly from rule-less, scattered sets than the model's interval/rule mixture, observed < null means more narrowly.
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_set_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets after 3+ example sets containing both odd and even numbers (no parity rule fits); observed > null means people generalise more broadly from rule-less, scattered sets than the model's interval/rule mixture, observed < null means more narrowly.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    par = ex % 2
    hasodd = par.eq(1).any(axis=1)
    haseven = par.eq(0).any(axis=1)
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & hasodd & haseven & ~inset
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float)[m].mean())

results.name: example_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets identical to one of the shown examples; observed < null means people reject already-seen examples more often than the model (which predicts near-certain yes minus lapse), observed > null means less.

results.name: within_set_magnitude_slope
results.description: OLS slope (per 100 units) of yes response on target value after demeaning both rating and target within each number_set, non-example targets only; observed < null means people favour smaller targets (a small-number bias) more than the model, observed > null means they favour larger targets.
results.code:
# name: within_set_magnitude_slope
# description: OLS slope (per 100 units) of yes response on target value after demeaning both rating and target within each number_set, non-example targets only; observed < null means people favour smaller targets (a small-number bias) more than the model, observed > null means they favour larger targets.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = ~inset
    g = df["number_set"][m]
    tt = t[m] / 100.0
    rr = df["rating"].astype(float)[m]
    tc = tt - tt.groupby(g).transform("mean")
    rc = rr - rr.groupby(g).transform("mean")
    den = float((tc * tc).sum())
    if den <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((tc * rc).sum() / den)

results.name: parity_rule_distance_gradient
results.description: Among 2+ example sets whose examples all share parity, for parity-matching non-example targets, yes rate within 10 of the nearest example minus yes rate 25+ away; observed > null means people's rule-consistent generalisation decays with numerical distance more than the model's flat rule extensions, observed < null means less decay.
results.code:
# name: parity_rule_distance_gradient
# description: Among 2+ example sets whose examples all share parity, for parity-matching non-example targets, yes rate within 10 of the nearest example minus yes rate 25+ away; observed > null means people's rule-consistent generalisation decays with numerical distance more than the model's flat rule extensions, observed < null means less decay.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    par = ex % 2
    allodd = (par.eq(1) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1)
    alleven = (par.eq(0) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1)
    match = (allodd & (t % 2 == 1)) | (alleven & (t % 2 == 0))
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    dist = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & match & ~inset
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = r[base & (dist <= 10)]
    b = r[base & (dist >= 25)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: digit_reversal_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets whose two digits are the reverse of some example's (e.g. 38 for example 83; single digits treated as 0x); observed > null means people treat digit-reversed numbers as similar more than the model's digit-containment rules predict, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets whose two digits are the reverse of some example's (e.g. 38 for example 83; single digits treated as 0x); observed > null means people treat digit-reversed numbers as similar more than the model's digit-containment rules predict, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    rev = (ex % 10) * 10 + (ex // 10)
    inset = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = rev.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1) & ~inset
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float)[m].mean())
